intro.en: Core gross surgical pathology specimens commonly displayed in practical examination jars and spotter viva voce stations for final-year MBBS candidates, detailing diagnostic features, clinical pathology, and examiner questions.

items.summary: Formalin-fixed specimen of the vermiform appendix displaying swollen turgid contour, congested serosa, and purulent fibrinous exudate.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Elongated cylindrical tubular structure measuring 7 to 9 cm in length with a swollen, thickened, rigid wall.
Serosal external surface appears deeply congested, dull, and covered with patches of yellowish-white fibrinous exudate.
Cut section reveals a thickened oedematous appendiceal wall with narrowed lumen containing pus or an obstructing fecolith.
Mucosal lining demonstrates focal ulcerations, haemorrhagic petechiae, and friability.

blocks.title: Etiopathology and complications
bullets: Luminal obstruction is the initiating event: fecolith (commonest in adults) or lymphoid hyperplasia (commonest in children).
Obstruction causes mucus accumulation, raised intraluminal pressure, venous stasis, and secondary bacterial invasion.
Untreated acute suppurative appendicitis progresses to gangrenous appendicitis, perforation, and peritonitis.
Other clinical outcomes include appendicular mass (phlegmon) and appendicular abscess walled off by omentum.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: The vermiform appendix receives its arterial blood supply from the appendicular artery, an end-artery of the ileocolic artery.
Because the appendicular artery is a terminal branch, thrombosis rapidly precipitates ischaemic necrosis and gangrene.
Histopathological hallmark of acute appendicitis is neutrophilic infiltration through the muscularis propria into the wall.

viva.q: What is the histological gold standard criterion to confirm acute appendicitis?
viva.a: Presence of polymorphonuclear neutrophils actively infiltrating the muscularis propria layer of the appendiceal wall.

viva.q: Why is the appendix particularly prone to early ischaemic gangrene and perforation?
viva.a: Because its arterial supply, the appendicular artery, is a terminal end-artery; raised intraluminal pressure readily occludes microvascular flow, causing rapid transmural ischaemic necrosis.

viva.q: What are the common anatomical positions of the vermiform appendix?
viva.a: Retrocaecal (most common, approximately 65%), pelvic (approximately 30%), subcaecal, pre-ileal, post-ileal, and promontoric positions.

image.brief: Formalin-fixed pathology specimen jar containing a swollen, enlarged vermiform appendix with dull congested serosa and a cut surface revealing a thickened wall and luminal fecolith.

items.summary: Formalin-fixed specimen of the vermiform appendix demonstrating dusky green to black transmural necrosis with friable wall and focal perforation.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Markedly swollen, discoloured vermiform appendix displaying patchy or confluent dark green, brown, or purplish-black discolouration.
Transmural tissue friability with a focal wall defect or blowout perforation, typically along the antimesenteric border.
Lumen contains foul-smelling necrotic debris, inspissated faecolith, and dark blood.
Mesoappendix appears heavily congested, thickened, and oedematous with thrombosed appendicular vascular branches.

blocks.title: Pathophysiology and perforation site
bullets: Results from progressive tissue ischemia when intraluminal pressure exceeds capillary perfusion pressure.
Perforation typically occurs at the antimesenteric border near the tip or mid-body where collateral flow is poorest.
Can lead to generalised peritonitis, localized appendicular abscess, pelvic abscess, or portal pyaemia (pylephlebitis).
Pylephlebitis involves suppurative thrombosis of the portal vein leading to multiple pyogenic liver abscesses.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Sudden cessation of colicky pain followed by diffuse dull ache indicates perforation releasing luminal tension.
Emergency laparoscopic or open appendicectomy with peritoneal lavage is required to prevent widespread intra-abdominal sepsis.
Postoperative pelvic collection should be monitored clinically with temperature charts and ultrasound.

viva.q: Why does perforation in acute gangrenous appendicitis usually occur at the antimesenteric border?
viva.a: The antimesenteric border is the watershed zone furthest from the mesoappendicular vascular arcade, making it most susceptible to ischaemic necrosis.

viva.q: What is pylephlebitis and how does it relate to gangrenous appendicitis?
viva.a: Suppurative thrombophlebitis of the portal venous system secondary to appendicular infection, leading to high-spiking rigors, jaundice, and multiple hepatic abscesses.

viva.q: What clinical phenomenon occurs when an inflamed tense appendix perforates?
viva.a: The intense colicky pain suddenly abates as intraluminal pressure drops, only to be followed hours later by diffuse peritonitis and persistent generalized pain.

image.brief: Formalin-fixed museum jar showing a friable, dark green-black necrotic vermiform appendix with a distinct 5 mm perforation defect on its antimesenteric surface and thrombosed mesoappendix.

title.en: Mucocele of the appendix gross specimen

items.summary: Gross specimen of the vermiform appendix demonstrating marked cystic dilatation of the lumen filled with clear, viscous, gelatinous mucin.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Globular or sausage-shaped cystic enlargement of the distal appendix with a smooth, tense, translucent external wall.
Wall is markedly attenuated, thin, and stretched, resembling a transparent glistening sac.
Cut section reveals an expanded cavity filled with thick, tenacious, gelatinous mucus without foul odour.
Surrounding tissues are devoid of acute inflammatory congestion unless secondary bacterial infection has supervened.

blocks.title: Histological classification and clinical risk
bullets: Four underlying histological types: mucosal hyperplasia, simple retention cyst, mucinous cystadenoma, and mucinous cystadenocarcinoma.
Mucinous cystadenoma (low-grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasm, LAMN) is the most frequent neoplastic subtype.
Iatrogenic rupture during surgical handling or spontaneous rupture leads to pseudomyxoma peritonei.
Pseudomyxoma peritonei is characterized by peritoneal dissemination of mucin-secreting epithelium and gelatinous ascites ('jelly belly').

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Meticulous non-touch surgical technique without grasping the appendix wall is essential to prevent intra-abdominal spillage.
If the caecal base is clear, appendicectomy with clear margin is sufficient; if the base is involved, caecectomy or right hemicolectomy is required.
Concurrent ovarian mucinous tumors must be carefully excluded in female patients.

viva.q: What is pseudomyxoma peritonei and how is it related to mucocele of the appendix?
viva.a: A condition caused by rupture of an appendiceal mucinous neoplasm, seeding mucus-producing epithelial cells throughout the peritoneum resulting in abundant gelatinous deposits.

viva.q: What are the four histopathological categories of appendiceal mucocele?
viva.a: Retention cyst, mucosal hyperplasia, mucinous cystadenoma (low-grade mucinous neoplasm), and mucinous cystadenocarcinoma.

viva.q: What critical surgical principle must be followed when resecting a suspected appendiceal mucocele?
viva.a: Gentle handling without direct instrument traction or puncture of the wall, ensuring an intact capsule to eliminate the risk of peritoneal mucin spillage.

image.brief: Formalin-fixed pathology specimen showing a sausage-shaped, translucent cystic dilatation of the vermiform appendix measuring 8 by 4 cm filled with clear gelatinous mucinous fluid.

items.summary: Opened cholecystectomy specimen demonstrating a thickened, fibrotic gallbladder wall containing multiple faceted, yellowish-brown mixed gallstones.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Opened gallbladder specimen demonstrating a thickened, leathery, fibrotic wall measuring greater than 3 mm in thickness.
Multiple faceted, polyhedral yellowish-brown calculi with flattened interlocking surfaces fitting together snugly.
Mucosal surface is granular, trabeculated, and bile-stained with effacement of normal delicate rugae.
Cut section of a calculus shows alternating concentric laminations of cholesterol, calcium bilirubinate, and protein matrix.

blocks.title: Pathogenesis and composition
bullets: Mixed stones account for approximately 75% to 80% of all gallstones encountered in Indian clinical practice.
Formed by biliary stasis, supersaturation of bile with cholesterol, and chronic low-grade bacterial infection.
Faceted shape develops because multiple stones grow simultaneously in close contact inside a contracting gallbladder.
Radio-opacity: approximately 15% to 20% are radio-opaque due to adequate calcium salt content.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Ultrasonography is the definitive diagnostic modality of choice, showing echogenic foci with posterior acoustic shadowing.
Complications include biliary colic, acute cholecystitis, empyema, mucocele, gallstone pancreatitis, and gallstone ileus.
Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the surgical standard of care for symptomatic cholelithiasis.

viva.q: Why do mixed gallstones acquire a faceted, polyhedral shape?
viva.a: Because multiple stones form together in the contracting gallbladder, continually rubbing against one another and flattening their opposing contacting surfaces.

viva.q: What are the three cardinal physical factors leading to cholesterol gallstone formation?
viva.a: Cholesterol supersaturation of bile, accelerated crystal nucleation, and gallbladder hypomotility leading to biliary stasis.

viva.q: What is the wall thickness criterion on ultrasound indicating chronic cholecystitis?
viva.a: Gallbladder wall thickness exceeding 3 mm in a fasting state, accompanied by mural fibrosis and loss of mucosal layering.

image.brief: Gross pathology jar showing a bisected gallbladder with a 4 mm thickened fibrous wall containing twenty faceted yellowish-brown gallstones with interlocking flat surfaces.

items.summary: Opened gallbladder specimen containing a large, solitary, oval or rounded yellowish-white cholesterol stone with crystalline cut surface.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Solitary, large, oval, spherical, or barrel-shaped calculus typically measuring 2 to 4 cm in major diameter.
External surface is creamy-yellow or pale white, finely nodular or smooth like a mulberry.
Fractured or cut surface exhibits glistening, translucent, radiating crystalline needles arranged like spokes of a wheel.
Gallbladder wall is typically thin or mildly thickened; mucosa may show chronic inflammatory or cholesterolosis changes.

blocks.title: Etiology and clinical complications
bullets: Composed of pure cholesterol (over 90% to 95% cholesterol content by weight).
Forms in uninfected, sterile bile due to hepatic hypersecretion of cholesterol exceeding micellar solubilisation capacity.
Pure cholesterol stones are radiolucent on plain radiographs unless secondary superficial calcium precipitation occurs.
A large solitary stone can erode into the duodenum via cholecystoduodenal fistula, producing mechanical gallstone ileus.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Risk factors conform to the traditional mnemonic: Fat, Female, Fertile, Forty, and Flatulent.
Impacted stone in Hartmann pouch or cystic duct causes mucocele of the gallbladder or Mirizzi syndrome.
Mirizzi syndrome occurs when extrinsic compression from the impacted stone causes common hepatic duct obstruction and jaundice.

viva.q: What does the cut surface of a pure cholesterol gallstone look like?
viva.a: It reveals glistening, pale translucent crystals arranged in a characteristic radial spoke-like architecture radiating from a central core.

viva.q: What is gallstone ileus and which type of stone is typically responsible?
viva.a: Mechanical small bowel obstruction caused by a large solitary stone eroding into the duodenum via a cholecystoduodenal fistula and impacting at the narrow ileocaecal valve.

viva.q: Why are pure cholesterol gallstones radiolucent on plain abdominal radiographs?
viva.a: Because pure cholesterol has low physical atomic density and lacks sufficient radio-dense calcium salts to attenuate X-ray beams.

image.brief: Opened cholecystectomy specimen demonstrating a single, large 3 cm oval, pale yellowish crystalline cholesterol gallstone resting within the gallbladder lumen.

items.summary: Opened gallbladder specimen revealing numerous small, irregular, black or dark brown, brittle, non-faceted pigment calculi.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Multiple small, jet-black or dark greenish-brown calculi ranging from 2 to 5 mm in diameter.
Irregular, mulberry-like, spicular, or amorphous shapes without flat faceted surfaces.
Stones are brittle, hard, and fragile, crushing easily under manual pressure into gritty soot-like particles.
Amorphous, non-crystalline, homogeneous dark brown or black cut surface without radial architecture.

blocks.title: Black versus brown pigment stones
bullets: Black pigment stones: form in sterile gallbladder bile in chronic haemolysis (thalassaemia, sickle cell, spherocytosis) and cirrhosis.
Composed of insoluble polymerised calcium bilirubinate, calcium phosphate, and glycoprotein matrix.
Brown pigment stones: form in the bile ducts secondary to bacterial or parasitic biliary infection (Clonorchis, Ascaris).
Bacterial beta-glucuronidase hydrolyses conjugated bilirubin glucuronide into free unconjugated bilirubin, precipitating calcium bilirubinate.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Black pigment stones are radio-opaque in 50% to 60% of cases due to associated calcium phosphate and carbonate salts.
Patients with hereditary spherocytosis or thalassaemia major undergoing splenectomy should have concurrent cholecystectomy if stones are present.
Brown pigment stones are frequently primary bile duct stones, recurring after cholecystectomy.

viva.q: What clinical conditions predispose to black pigment gallstone formation?
viva.a: Chronic haemolytic states (thalassaemia, hereditary spherocytosis, sickle cell anaemia) and liver cirrhosis, generating excessive unconjugated bilirubin excretion in bile.

viva.q: How do brown pigment stones differ from black pigment stones in pathogenesis and location?
viva.a: Brown stones form in bile ducts due to bacterial infection and beta-glucuronidase production; black stones form in the gallbladder in sterile bile from chronic haemolysis.

viva.q: Why are black pigment stones more often radio-opaque than cholesterol stones?
viva.a: Because black pigment stones incorporate significant concentrations of calcium phosphate, calcium carbonate, and heavy metal salts into their matrix.

image.brief: Pathology jar showing a bisected gallbladder containing dozens of tiny, irregular, jet-black, spicular, mulberry-shaped pigment gallstones with dark bile residue.

items.summary: Opened gallbladder specimen displaying a reticular network of fine yellow lipid speckles against a congested red velvety mucosa.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Mucosal surface exhibits an intricate, bright yellow reticular pattern resembling ripe strawberry seeds against a red background.
Tiny, discrete, pinhead-sized bright yellow specks distributed along mucosal rugae.
Underlying gallbladder wall is usually thin, pliable, and non-fibrotic without marked thickening.
May be accompanied by small, pedunculated yellow mucosal polyps (cholesterol polyps).

blocks.title: Microscopic pathology and mechanism
bullets: Caused by abnormal accumulation of cholesterol esters and triglycerides within the cytoplasm of lamina propria macrophages (foam cells).
Excessive cholesterol in bile is absorbed by surface epithelial cells and esterified, accumulating in subepithelial histiocytes.
Enlarged, lipid-laden mucosal folds project into the lumen as polypoid fronds, visible grossly as yellow dots.
Not associated with hypercholesterolaemia or generalized systemic lipid storage disorders.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Usually an incidental finding discovered during cholecystectomy or routine pathological grossing.
Can cause biliary colic if fragile cholesterol polyps detach and temporarily obstruct the cystic duct.
Differentiate from true adenomatous polyps: cholesterol polyps are multiple, non-neoplastic, and carry zero malignant potential.

viva.q: Why is cholesterolosis called the 'strawberry gallbladder'?
viva.a: Because the yellow punctate lipid deposits against the hyperaemic, congested red background of mucosal rugae visually resemble the surface seeds of a ripe strawberry.

viva.q: What is the histological hallmark of cholesterolosis?
viva.a: Aggregations of foamy, lipid-laden histiocytes (macrophages) packed with cholesterol esters engorging the lamina propria cores of the mucosal villi.

viva.q: Do cholesterol polyps carry malignant potential?
viva.a: No, cholesterol polyps are non-neoplastic pseudopolyps formed by lipid accumulation and have no potential for malignant transformation.

image.brief: Opened cholecystectomy specimen showing a velvety red mucosal lining covered with a fine reticular meshwork of bright yellow punctate lipid speckles (strawberry appearance).

title.en: Carcinoma of the gallbladder gross specimen

items.summary: Resected gallbladder specimen showing dense, irregular, greyish-white thickening of the fundus and wall infiltrating into adjacent liver parenchyma.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Asymmetrical, focal or diffuse, dense greyish-white cartilaginous thickening of the gallbladder wall, typically at the fundus or neck.
Wall is rigid, firm to hard (scirrhous) with complete loss of normal mucosal rugae and layered architecture.
Cut surface is greyish-white, gritty, and homogeneous, directly infiltrating into the adherent wedge of liver tissue.
Gallstones are present within the contracted gallbladder lumen in 70% to 80% of resected surgical specimens.

blocks.title: Epidemiology, risk factors, and spread
bullets: Marked geographical predilection in northern and eastern India (Gangetic belt), with female to male ratio of 3 to 1.
Primary risk factor is chronic cholelithiasis, particularly large stones (>3 cm), anomalous pancreaticobiliary ductal junction, and porcelain gallbladder.
Histologically, adenocarcinoma accounts for over 85% to 90% of cases.
Spreads early by direct contiguous invasion into the liver bed (Segments IVb and V) and lymphatic drainage to cystic and pericholedochal nodes.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Porcelain gallbladder (extensive intramural mural calcification) carries a 10% to 20% risk of gallbladder cancer, warranting prophylactic cholecystectomy.
Incidental gallbladder cancer found after routine laparoscopic cholecystectomy requires radical reresection if T1b or deeper.
Radical cholecystectomy entails en bloc wedge resection of liver bed (Segments IVb and V) plus regional lymphadenectomy.

viva.q: What are the major risk factors for carcinoma of the gallbladder in India?
viva.a: Longstanding cholelithiasis with large stones, female gender, residence in northern/eastern Gangetic river basins, porcelain gallbladder, and anomalous pancreaticobiliary union.

viva.q: What does radical cholecystectomy comprise for gallbladder carcinoma?
viva.a: En bloc resection of the gallbladder along with a 2 cm wedge of liver tissue from segments IVb and V, plus skeletonisation lymphadenectomy of the hepatoduodenal ligament.

viva.q: What is an incidental gallbladder carcinoma and what is the management for a T1b lesion?
viva.a: Carcinoma detected unexpectedly on histology after cholecystectomy for benign disease; T1b invading muscle requires re-exploration for radical liver wedge resection and nodal clearance.

image.brief: Gross specimen jar showing a bisected gallbladder with a 1.5 cm thick, hard, greyish-white infiltrative mass in the fundus directly invading into an attached wedge of brown liver parenchyma.

items.summary: Partial gastrectomy specimen demonstrating a large, irregular malignant ulcer on the lesser curvature with rolled, everted edges and dirty necrotic floor.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Large, irregular or oval ulcerated lesion measuring greater than 3 cm in diameter, commonly situated on the lesser curvature or antrum.
Elevated, rolled, everted, and indurated margins (crater-like lip) with abrupt transition to surrounding mucosa.
Floor of the ulcer is deep, dirty, slough-covered, and nodular with brownish-red necrotic debris.
Surrounding normal gastric mucosal rugae terminate abruptly (amputated) at the indurated margin of the tumour.

blocks.title: Borrnann gross classification and etiology
bullets: Borrnann type II represents an ulcerated, circumscribed carcinoma with sharp, raised borders.
Borrnann type III represents an ulcerated infiltrative lesion with diffuse invasion into the adjacent gastric wall.
Etiological factors include chronic Helicobacter pylori gastritis, dietary nitrosamines, smoked foods, pernicious anaemia, and blood group A.
Histologically divided into intestinal type (glandular, cohesive) and diffuse type (signet-ring cells, poorly differentiated) by Lauren classification.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Distinguish from benign gastric ulcer: benign ulcer has punched-out, clean margins with radiating mucosal folds meeting the ulcer edge.
Metastatic routes: direct, lymphatic (Troisier sign: left supraclavicular Virchow node), haematogenous (liver), transcoelomic (Krukenberg tumour).
Standard curative resection is radical subtotal gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy and Roux-en-Y gastrojejunostomy.

viva.q: How do you distinguish a malignant gastric ulcer from a chronic benign gastric ulcer on gross inspection?
viva.a: Malignant ulcer has rolled, everted edges, necrotic dirty floor, indurated base, and amputated mucosal folds; benign ulcer has punched-out edges and radiating folds reaching the crater.

viva.q: What is Troisier sign and Virchow node?
viva.a: Enlargement of the left supraclavicular lymph node (Virchow node) due to metastatic spread of abdominal malignancy (especially gastric cancer) via the thoracic duct.

viva.q: What is a Krukenberg tumour and what is its histological hallmark?
viva.a: Bilateral ovarian metastases from an abdominal primary (usually gastric carcinoma), characterised histologically by mucin-producing signet ring adenocarcinoma cells.

image.brief: Partial gastrectomy specimen pinned flat displaying a 4 by 3 cm irregular ulcer on the lesser curvature with thickened, rolled everted margins and a necrotic slough-covered floor.

items.summary: Total gastrectomy specimen displaying diffuse circumferential fibrous thickening and leathery rigidity of the gastric wall with obliteration of mucosal rugae.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Gastric specimen is contracted, shrunken, and small with a rigid, non-pliable 'leather-bottle' wall consistency.
Cut section demonstrates diffuse, uniform transmural thickening of the gastric wall measuring 1 to 2 cm in thickness.
Normal delicate mucosal rugal folds are completely flattened, effaced, and ironed out with a pearly-white fibrous cut surface.
Conspicuous absence of discrete exophytic polypoid growth or localized ulcer crater; entire stomach behaves as a rigid conduit.

blocks.title: Microscopic features and Lauren classification
bullets: Represents Borrnann type IV diffuse infiltrative carcinoma, corresponding to Lauren diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma.
Characterized by individual or small clusters of malignant signet-ring cells diffusely infiltrating all layers of the gastric wall.
Malignant cells induce an intense reactive desmoplastic stromal fibrous reaction (desmoplasia), accounting for extreme wall rigidity.
Signet-ring cells contain abundant intracellular mucin that pushes the hyperchromatic nucleus to the cell periphery.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Often affects younger patients and is linked with hereditary diffuse gastric cancer (germline CDH1 E-cadherin mutations).
Endoscopic mucosal punch biopsy may yield false-negative results because the tumour infiltrates deep in the submucosa and muscularis.
Prognosis is poor due to early transmural peritoneal dissemination and extensive nodal involvement; requires total gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy.

viva.q: What causes the extreme wall thickening and rigidity in linitis plastica?
viva.a: Diffuse infiltration of signet-ring adenocarcinoma cells throughout the submucosa and muscularis, which incites intense reactive fibroblastic desmoplasia.

viva.q: Why can endoscopic mucosal biopsies produce false-negative results in linitis plastica?
viva.a: Because the tumor preferentially infiltrates the submucosal and muscular layers while sparing the superficial mucosal epithelium, requiring deep snare or bite-on-bite biopsies.

viva.q: Which germline gene mutation is responsible for hereditary diffuse gastric cancer?
viva.a: Mutations in the CDH1 gene encoding the cellular adhesion protein E-cadherin, associated with diffuse gastric cancer and lobular breast carcinoma.

image.brief: Total gastrectomy specimen cut longitudinally demonstrating a rigid, contracted, tubular stomach with a uniformly thickened 1.5 cm white fibrous wall and completely flattened mucosa.

title.en: Annular carcinoma of the colon gross specimen

items.summary: Resected segment of sigmoid colon demonstrating an annular, napkin-ring constricting tumor with circumferential luminal narrowing and proximal hypertrophy.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Resected segment of large bowel displaying a tight, short (3 to 4 cm), circumferential, napkin-ring constriction.
Tumour encircles the entire circumference of the bowel wall, severely stenosing the intestinal lumen down to a narrow slit.
Cut section shows an infiltrating, firm, greyish-white tumour replacing the muscular wall and encroaching into pericolic fat.
Proximal colon demonstrates marked luminal dilatation, muscular hypertrophy, and oedematous hyperaemic mucosa.

blocks.title: Clinical anatomy and presentation
bullets: Predominates in the left colon: descending colon, sigmoid, and rectosigmoid junction where stool is semi-solid.
Presents clinically with altered bowel habits, increasing constipation alternating with diarrhoea, colicky pain, and obstruction.
Perforation may occur either at the tumor site (diastatic perforation) or more commonly in the thin-walled, distended caecum.
Pathological staging follows the Dukes classification or modern TNM staging system.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Surgical margin rule: a minimum of 5 cm proximal and distal bowel clearance with high ligation of the vascular pedicle is standard.
For sigmoid carcinoma, oncological resection is anterior resection or sigmoid colectomy with high tie of inferior mesenteric artery.
Emergency presentation with complete obstruction may require Hartmann procedure or stenting as a bridge to elective surgery.

viva.q: Why do left-sided colonic carcinomas present with obstruction much earlier than right-sided carcinomas?
viva.a: The left colon has a narrower lumen, thicker wall, and contains solid formed faeces, whereas the right colon is wide with liquid contents.

viva.q: What is a Hartmann procedure and when is it indicated?
viva.a: Resection of the rectosigmoid lesion, closure of the rectal stump, and exteriorisation of the proximal descending colon as an end colostomy in acute obstruction or perforation.

viva.q: What is the minimum safe distal resection margin for colonic carcinoma?
viva.a: A minimum of 5 cm clear longitudinal margin of healthy bowel wall proximal and distal to the tumour to ensure complete clearance of intramural spread.

image.brief: Resected segment of sigmoid colon slit open longitudinally displaying a 3 cm short, annular constricting tumor encircling the lumen like a napkin ring with dilated proximal bowel.

items.summary: Right hemicolectomy specimen cut open showing a large, exophytic, polypoid, friable caulifower-like mass projecting from the caecal mucosal wall.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Resected right hemicolectomy specimen including terminal ileum, caecum, ascending colon, and appendix.
Large, bulky, exophytic, caulifower-like polypoid mass measuring 5 to 8 cm protruding from the medial caecal wall into the lumen.
Surface of the tumour is irregular, friable, ulcerated, and necrotic with areas of dark haemorrhagic slough.
Despite its large size, the wide lumen of the caecum remains patent without complete mechanical luminal obstruction.

blocks.title: Clinical presentation and pathophysiology
bullets: Presents indolently with microcytic hypochromic iron deficiency anaemia due to chronic, insidious occult blood loss.
Other presentations: palpable, non-tender, mobile right iliac fossa lump, weakness, anorexia, and unexplained weight loss.
Rarely causes acute intestinal obstruction because the caecal lumen is large (calibre 7 to 9 cm) and the contents are fluid.
Associated with microsatellite instability (MSI-high) and Lynch syndrome (hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer).

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Every adult male or postmenopausal woman presenting with unexplained iron deficiency anaemia must undergo colonoscopy.
Oncological surgical treatment is radical right hemicolectomy with high ligation of ileocolic and right colic vascular pedicles.
Specimen must yield a minimum of 12 regional lymph nodes for accurate pathological nodal staging.

viva.q: What is the classic clinical triad of symptoms in a patient with carcinoma of the caecum?
viva.a: Unexplained microcytic iron deficiency anaemia, weakness/weight loss, and a palpable non-tender lump in the right iliac fossa.

viva.q: Why do caecal carcinomas grow to such large sizes before causing symptoms?
viva.a: Because the caecum has the largest diameter in the colon, a distensible thin wall, and contains liquid chyme that easily bypasses exophytic masses.

viva.q: What anatomical structures are resected in a standard radical right hemicolectomy?
viva.a: Distal 10 to 15 cm of terminal ileum, caecum, appendix, ascending colon, hepatic flexure, and proximal third of transverse colon with regional mesentery.

image.brief: Right hemicolectomy gross specimen cut open displaying a 6 cm bulky, exophytic, caulifower-like friable tumour arising from the caecal wall adjacent to the ileocaecal valve.

items.summary: Modified radical mastectomy specimen with skin elliptical paddle, nipple-areola complex, and cut surface revealing an infiltrative, gritty, grey-white tumour.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Resected breast specimen covered by an elliptical skin paddle incorporating the central nipple-areola complex and axillary tail.
Cut surface reveals a stellate, irregular, non-encapsulated, greyish-white firm to hard tumour infiltrating surrounding yellow fibrofatty parenchyma.
Gritty sensation on slicing with a scalpel, resembling the crisp texture of cutting an unripe pear or water chestnut.
Chalky yellow streaks and punctate calcifications visible in the core of the scirrhous fibrous stroma.
Surface puckering: gross tethering and retraction of overlying skin or retraction and inversion of the nipple.

blocks.title: Microscopic features and Nottingham grading
bullets: Most common histological type is invasive breast carcinoma of no special type (invasive ductal carcinoma, IDC), accounting for 70% to 80%.
Nottingham histological grading evaluates tubule formation, nuclear pleomorphism, and mitotic frequency to assign Grades 1, 2, or 3.
Immunohistochemistry (IHC) profiling assesses Estrogen Receptor (ER), Progesterone Receptor (PR), HER2/neu, and Ki-67 proliferation index.
Triple-negative breast cancer (ER-, PR-, HER2-negative) exhibits aggressive biological behaviour and lacks targeted endocrine therapies.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Skin changes: peau d'orange is caused by cutaneous dermal lymphatic permeation and dermal oedema tethered at hair follicles.
Axillary lymph node status is the single most powerful prognostic indicator for long-term overall and disease-free survival.
Level I (lateral to pectoralis minor), Level II (behind pectoralis minor), and Level III (medial to pectoralis minor) axillary nodal stations.

viva.q: What produces the gritty sensation when cutting through an invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast?
viva.a: Abundant desmoplastic fibrous connective tissue stroma interspersed with microscopic foci of calcification within the tumour matrix.

viva.q: What is the mechanism responsible for peau d'orange appearance of the skin overlying breast carcinoma?
viva.a: Obstruction of subdermal lymphatics by malignant emboli producing cutaneous oedema; the swollen skin is tethered down at sweat glands and hair follicles.

viva.q: What are the anatomical boundaries of Berg axillary lymph node levels?
viva.a: Level I lies lateral to pectoralis minor; Level II lies deep behind pectoralis minor; Level III lies medial and superior to pectoralis minor.

image.brief: Gross pathology slice of a modified radical mastectomy specimen showing an elliptical skin island, inverted nipple, and a 3 cm stellate, greyish-white scirrhous mass in yellow fat.

title.en: Fibroadenoma of the breast gross specimen

items.summary: Well-circumscribed, encapsulated, firm, lobulated greyish-white breast lump specimen showing slit-like curved clefts on a bulging whorled cut surface.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Sharply circumscribed, rounded or ovoid, bosselated or lobulated mass measuring 2 to 4 cm in diameter.
True complete fibrous capsule enclosing the entire tumour, allowing it to shell out cleanly from surrounding breast parenchyma.
Firm, rubbery, elastic consistency on palpation.
Cut surface is greyish-white, glistening, and characteristically bulges above the cut plane of the capsule.
Displays a whorled trabecular pattern with curved, slit-like linear clefts representing compressed ductal spaces.

blocks.title: Histology and clinical characteristics
bullets: Biphasic benign fibroepithelial neoplasm composed of proliferating stromal connective tissue and epithelial glandular elements.
Histological patterns: intracanalicular (stroma compresses ducts into clefts) and pericanalicular (stroma surrounds open patent ducts).
Clinically known as the 'breast mouse' because of its extreme slip-like mobility within the breast substance.
Most prevalent benign breast disorder in young women aged 15 to 30 years, driven by relative oestrogen sensitivity.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Giant fibroadenoma is defined as a benign fibroadenoma exceeding 5 cm in diameter or 500 grams in weight.
Distinguish from phyllodes tumour: phyllodes tumour occurs in older women (40+), grows rapidly, and exhibits stromal hypercellularity and leaf-like clefts.
Triple assessment (clinical examination, ultrasound, and core-needle biopsy) confirms the benign diagnosis.

viva.q: Why does the cut surface of a resected fibroadenoma bulge above the capsular plane?
viva.a: Because the tense, cellular fibroepithelial stroma inside the true capsule is under physical elastic tension, protruding outward once the capsule is divided.

viva.q: Why is a fibroadenoma clinically referred to as a 'breast mouse'?
viva.a: Because it is completely encapsulated, non-infiltrative, and slips freely and easily under the examining fingers within the mobile breast tissue.

viva.q: How do you differentiate a large fibroadenoma from a benign phyllodes tumour?
viva.a: Phyllodes tumours occur in older women, exhibit rapid growth, and show hypercellular leaf-like stromal architecture with potential for local recurrence.

image.brief: Gross pathology specimen showing a well-encapsulated, firm, lobulated 3 cm oval grey-white breast mass whose cut surface bulges outward with fine slit-like clefts.

items.summary: Subtotal or total thyroidectomy specimen displaying asymmetric, lobulated enlargement with multiple colloid nodules, fibrous septa, and cystic degeneration.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Asymmetrically enlarged thyroid gland showing bosselated, lobulated, irregular external surface with preservation of butterfly contour.
Cut surface displays multiple, variable-sized, well-demarcated nodules ranging from a few millimetres to several centimetres.
Nodules contain amber, translucent, gelatinous or honey-like colloid material separated by pale whitish fibrous bands.
Secondary degenerative changes are prominent: focal cystic degeneration, old brownish haemorrhage, fibrosis, and gritty calcification.

blocks.title: Etiopathology and physiological evolution
bullets: Originates as physiological diffuse hyperplasia in response to persistent TSH stimulation (iodine deficiency or goitrogens).
Cycles of fluctuating TSH stimulation and involution lead to heterogeneous autonomous follicular growth and nodule formation.
Iodine-deficient endemic goitre belt includes the Himalayan foothills, northern plains, and central plateau in India.
Toxic multinodular goitre (Plummer disease) occurs when one or more autonomous nodules develop TSH-receptor mutations, producing thyrotoxicosis.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Sudden painful enlargement of a nodule indicates acute intranodular haemorrhage.
Compressive symptoms include dyspnoea (tracheal deviation/compression), dysphagia (oesophageal pressure), and stridor.
Total thyroidectomy is the surgical procedure of choice today to prevent recurrence and eliminate occult malignancy risk.

viva.q: What causes the varied nodular appearance and degenerative changes in multinodular goitre?
viva.a: Repeated cycles of TSH-induced follicular hyperplasia alternating with involution, causing follicular rupture, haemorrhage, fibrosis, and cyst formation.

viva.q: What is the significance of sudden painful swelling within a long-standing painless goitre?
viva.a: It usually signifies acute spontaneous intranodular haemorrhage into a pre-existing cyst or nodule, requiring reassurance and conservative management.

viva.q: What is Plummer disease?
viva.a: Toxic multinodular goitre, in which one or more autonomous hyperfunctioning thyroid nodules secrete thyroid hormones independently of TSH.

image.brief: Total thyroidectomy gross specimen displaying an enlarged, nodular gland with cut surfaces showing multiple amber-brown colloid nodules, cystic spaces, and pale fibrous bands.

title.en: Papillary carcinoma of the thyroid gland

items.summary: Thyroid lobectomy specimen demonstrating an ill-defined, solid grey-white infiltrative mass containing focal microcystic spaces, granular papillary fronds, and calcification.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Solid, unencapsulated or partially circumscribed, pale greyish-white firm mass infiltrating into the adjacent brownish thyroid parenchyma.
Cut surface exhibits a granular, finely papillary, or velvety texture with delicate, microscopic papillary projections.
Small cystic spaces containing brownish fluid and fine, gritty microcalcifications (corresponding to microscopic psammoma bodies).
Surrounding thyroid capsule may be tethered or penetrated by focal extrathyroidal tumour extension.

blocks.title: Microscopic hallmarks and biological behaviour
bullets: Most common malignant thyroid tumour, accounting for approximately 80% to 85% of all thyroid cancers.
Classic nuclear diagnostic features: Orphan Annie eye nuclei (ground-glass empty nuclei), intranuclear pseudoinclusions, and nuclear grooves.
Psammoma bodies: concentrically laminated, basophilic calcospherites representing necrotic calcified papillary tips.
Strong predilection for early lymphatic metastasis to central compartment (Level VI) and lateral cervical lymph nodes (Levels II to V).

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Cervical nodal metastasis does not drastically worsen the excellent overall 10-year survival rate (exceeding 90% to 95%).
Historically known as 'lateral aberrant thyroid' when a cystic cervical lymph node metastasis was mistaken for ectopic thyroid tissue.
Standard management: total thyroidectomy with central compartment neck dissection (Level VI), followed by radioactive iodine (RAI) ablation.

viva.q: What are the pathognomonic microscopic nuclear features of papillary thyroid carcinoma?
viva.a: Optically clear ground-glass nuclei (Orphan Annie eyes), intranuclear cytoplasmic pseudoinclusions, prominent nuclear grooves, and overlapping nuclei.

viva.q: What are psammoma bodies and what is their diagnostic relevance?
viva.a: Concentric, laminated round calcified structures formed by infarction and mineralisation of papillary tips, pathognomonic for papillary thyroid cancer.

viva.q: What was meant historically by the term 'lateral aberrant thyroid'?
viva.a: A lateral cystic neck mass originally thought to be ectopic thyroid tissue, now recognized as a cystic lymph node metastasis from an occult papillary thyroid cancer.

image.brief: Gross hemithyroidectomy specimen displaying a 2.5 cm solid, greyish-white infiltrative tumour in the upper pole with a granular cut surface and tiny gritty calcific specks.

title.en: Seminoma of the testis gross specimen

items.summary: Radical high inguinal orchidectomy specimen showing an enlarged testis occupied by a circumscribed, lobulated, fleshy, homogeneous creamy-white tumour.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Globularly enlarged testis with smooth, glistening, intact tunica albuginea; epididymis is flattened and stretched over the periphery.
Cut surface displays a uniform, homogeneous, fleshy, creamy-white or pale tan mass expanding the testicular substance.
Tumour is lobulated, divided into discrete rounded lobules by delicate, thin, translucent fibrous septa.
Conspicuous absence of extensive haemorrhage or cystic degeneration, which characterizes non-seminomatous tumours.

blocks.title: Demographics, markers, and spread
bullets: Most common pure testicular germ cell tumour, typically presenting in men aged 30 to 50 years with a painless testicular swelling.
Serum tumour markers: normal alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is mandatory; beta-hCG may be mildly elevated in under 10% (syncytiotrophoblastic cells).
Any elevation of serum AFP rules out pure seminoma and indicates non-seminomatous elements (yolk sac component).
Lymphatic spread travels primarily to retroperitoneal para-aortic lymph nodes at the level of the renal hilum (L2 level).

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Cryptorchidism (undescended testis) carries a 4 to 10 fold increased risk of seminoma, even following successful orchidopexy.
High inguinal orchidectomy with initial vascular clamping at the deep internal ring is the mandatory surgical approach; NEVER perform trans-scrotal biopsy.
Seminomas are exquisitely radiosensitive and chemosensitive (platinum-based regimens such as BEP).

viva.q: Why must a suspected testicular tumour never be approached through a scrotal incision or biopsied trans-scrotally?
viva.a: Scrotal violation disrupts the anatomical barrier and alters lymphatic drainage, causing premature tumour dissemination to superficial inguinal lymph nodes.

viva.q: What is the primary lymphatic landing zone for testicular malignancies?
viva.a: The retroperitoneal para-aortic and interaortocaval lymph nodes at the level of L1-L2, reflecting the embryological origin of the gonads near the kidneys.

viva.q: Can pure seminoma elevate serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)?
viva.a: No, pure seminoma never produces AFP; any documented elevation of AFP indicates the presence of non-seminomatous germ cell elements such as yolk sac tumour.

title.en: Teratoma of the testis gross specimen

items.summary: High inguinal orchidectomy specimen showing a grossly distorted testis with a variegated, multilocular cut surface containing cysts, solid areas, and cartilage.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Asymmetrically enlarged, distorted testis with bosselated, irregular contour and focal breeches of the tunica albuginea.
Cut surface is markedly variegated, heterogeneous, and chaotic in appearance, contrasting with the uniform appearance of seminoma.
Displays multiple multiloculated cysts of varying sizes containing clear serous fluid, gelatinous mucin, or sebaceous material.
Solid fleshy areas interspersed with opaque white cartilage islands, bone spicules, and extensive dark areas of haemorrhage and necrosis.

blocks.title: Demographics, markers, and classification
bullets: Affects younger males, typically presenting between 20 and 30 years of age with a rapidly enlarging testicular lump.
Classified into mature teratoma, immature teratoma, and teratoma with somatic-type malignancy.
Serum tumour markers are markedly elevated: alpha-fetoprotein (AFP, from yolk sac components) and beta-hCG (from choriocarcinoma).
Unlike in females where ovarian cystic teratoma is predominantly benign, all postpubertal testicular teratomas are clinically malignant.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Early haematogenous dissemination to the lungs ('cannonball metastases') and liver occurs earlier than in seminoma.
Radio-resistant compared with seminoma; requires multimodal chemotherapy (BEP: bleomycin, etoposide, cisplatin).
Residual retroperitoneal masses following chemotherapy warrant retroperitoneal lymph node dissection (RPLND) for teratoma clearance.

viva.q: Why is a postpubertal testicular teratoma considered malignant even if histologically composed of mature tissues?
viva.a: Because all postpubertal testicular teratomas harbour malignant genetic alterations (isochromosome 12p) and can metastasise regardless of mature histology.

viva.q: How does the gross appearance of testicular teratoma differ from seminoma?
viva.a: Teratoma has a variegated, cystic, haemorrhagic, and necrotic cut surface containing cartilage and mucin; seminoma is homogeneous, fleshy, and creamy-white.

viva.q: What role does retroperitoneal lymph node dissection (RPLND) play in non-seminomatous germ cell tumours?
viva.a: It resects residual retroperitoneal masses after chemotherapy, which often harbour mature teratoma (growing teratoma syndrome) or viable carcinoma.

image.brief: Gross orchidectomy specimen cut in half revealing a heterogeneous, variegated tumour with multiple small fluid-filled cysts, solid grey nodules, cartilage flecks, and focal haemorrhage.

items.summary: Radical nephrectomy specimen demonstrating a large, golden-yellow variegated mass arising from renal cortex with haemorrhage, necrosis, and cystic change.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Radical nephrectomy specimen including kidney, perirenal Gerota fascia, perinephric fat, and renal vascular pedicle.
Large, spherical, bosselated tumour typically arising eccentrically from the upper or lower renal cortical pole.
Cut surface exhibits a brilliant, characteristic golden-yellow colour interspersed with variegated areas of red haemorrhage and grey necrosis.
Well-demarcated from the remaining compressed, crescentic rim of normal reddish-brown renal parenchyma by a false capsule (pseudocapsule).
Renal vein may contain an intraluminal propagating tumour thrombus extending into the inferior vena cava.

blocks.title: Microscopic basis and classic triad
bullets: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma accounts for 75% to 80% of all renal malignancies, arising from proximal convoluted tubular epithelium.
Brilliant golden-yellow colour is produced by abundant intracellular neutral lipids and glycogen dissolved during processing, leaving clear cytoplasm.
Associated with deletion or inactivation of the VHL (von Hippel-Lindau) tumour suppressor gene on chromosome 3p.
Classic clinical triad of haematuria, flank pain, and palpable mass (too-late triad) is present in under 10% of modern cases.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Left-sided renal cell carcinoma can present with a sudden, non-reducible varicocele due to tumour thrombus blocking the left renal vein.
Radical nephrectomy involves early ligation of the renal artery and vein before mobilising the kidney to prevent haematogenous tumour embolisation.
Partial nephrectomy (nephron-sparing surgery) is standard for small renal masses under 4 cm (T1a).

viva.q: What gives clear cell renal cell carcinoma its characteristic golden-yellow gross appearance?
viva.a: The tumour cells are packed with abundant intracytoplasmic neutral lipids, cholesterol esters, and glycogen, imparting a bright golden-yellow hue.

viva.q: Why does a left-sided renal cell carcinoma cause a left-sided varicocele that fails to decompress on lying down?
viva.a: The left testicular vein drains at a right angle into the left renal vein; tumour thrombus occludes the junction, producing high retrograde venous pressure.

viva.q: What is the primary surgical step during radical nephrectomy to prevent intraoperative haematogenous embolisation?
viva.a: Early dissection and ligation of the renal artery followed by the renal vein before manipulating or mobilising the tumour-bearing kidney.

image.brief: Radical nephrectomy specimen cut in half demonstrating a 7 cm spherical, variegated golden-yellow cortical tumour with central red haemorrhagic necrosis in the upper renal pole.

items.summary: Markedly enlarged nephrectomy specimen whose external surface is completely replaced by innumerable thin-walled cysts of varying sizes.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Massive kidney specimen, often weighing several kilograms and measuring 20 to 30 cm in length, retaining a distorted reniform shape.
External cortical surface is bosselated, knobby, and completely riddled with hundreds of bulging, thin-walled cysts.
Cysts vary in diameter from a few millimetres to several centimetres and contain clear straw-coloured fluid, gelatinous fluid, or turbid brown blood.
Cut surface demonstrates complete effacement of normal corticomedullary demarcation, with cysts communicating throughout all nephron segments.
Remaining normal functional renal parenchyma is compressed into thin, atrophic fibrous bands between expanding cysts.

blocks.title: Genetics, extra-renal manifestations, and course
bullets: Autosomal dominant inheritance with high penetrance: PKD1 gene on chromosome 16 (85%) and PKD2 gene on chromosome 4 (15%).
Bilateral symmetrical involvement, typically presenting clinically in the third to fifth decades with hypertension and flank fullness.
Extra-renal manifestations: polycystic liver disease (commonest, 70%), berry aneurysms of circle of Willis (10% to 15%), and mitral valve prolapse.
Rupture of a cerebral berry aneurysm produces catastrophic subarachnoid haemorrhage.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Progresses relentlessly to end-stage renal disease (ESRD), requiring maintenance haemodialysis or renal transplantation.
Nephrectomy is reserved for intractable pain, recurrent severe urosepsis, refractory haematuria, or to create space for a renal allograft.
Tolvaptan (vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist) slows cyst growth and renal function decline in rapidly progressive ADPKD.

viva.q: What are the two major genes responsible for autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease?
viva.a: PKD1 on chromosome 16 encoding polycystin-1 (accounting for approximately 85% of cases) and PKD2 on chromosome 4 encoding polycystin-2 (approximately 15%).

viva.q: What is the most lethal extra-renal vascular complication associated with ADPKD?
viva.a: Rupture of intracranial saccular (berry) aneurysms in the circle of Willis, leading to fatal or disabling subarachnoid haemorrhage.

viva.q: What are the specific surgical indications for nephrectomy in ADPKD?
viva.a: Intractable pain, recurrent life-threatening cyst haemorrhage, refractory cyst infection/urosepsis, suspicion of malignancy, or space creation for renal transplant.

image.brief: Gross nephrectomy specimen showing a massively enlarged 22 cm kidney with external and cut surfaces completely replaced by hundreds of varying-sized thin-walled fluid cysts.

title.en: Indirect inguinal hernial sac gross specimen

items.summary: Excised peritoneal hernial sac specimen showing a pearly-white glistening serosal structure with a well-defined neck, body, fundus, and attached fibrofatty tissue.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Funnel-shaped, pear-shaped, or tubular membranous sac composed of glistening, pearly-white fibrous and peritoneal tissue.
Displays three distinct anatomical regions: a narrow constricted neck, an expanded body, and a rounded blind fundus.
Internal surface is smooth, shiny, and lined by simple squamous mesothelial cells.
Outer surface is irregular, adherent to wisps of cremasteric muscle fibres, internal spermatic fascia, and preperitoneal fat.
May contain adherent intra-abdominal contents such as a tongue of greater omentum (enterocele or omentocele).

blocks.title: Anatomical landmarks and relation to vessels
bullets: Indirect inguinal hernial sac represents a patent processus vaginalis entering via the deep (internal) inguinal ring.
Neck of the indirect sac lies strictly lateral to the inferior epigastric artery.
Direct inguinal hernia, by contrast, bulges directly forward through Hesselbach triangle medial to the inferior epigastric artery.
Spermatic cord structures (vas deferens and testicular vessels) lie intimately adherent to the posterior wall of the indirect sac.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: High ligation of the sac at the level of the deep inguinal ring (herniotomy) is the essential curative step in paediatric indirect hernia.
In adults, herniotomy is combined with posterior inguinal canal wall reinforcement (Lichtenstein tension-free mesh repair).
Sliding hernia (hernia en glissade) occurs when a retroperitoneal viscus (sigmoid colon, caecum, or bladder) forms part of the sac wall.

viva.q: What anatomical relationship differentiates an indirect from a direct inguinal hernia at operation?
viva.a: The neck of an indirect hernial sac lies lateral to the inferior epigastric artery; a direct hernia bulges medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.

viva.q: What is a sliding hernia (hernia en glissade)?
viva.a: A hernia in which an intra-abdominal retroperitoneal viscus, such as the caecum, sigmoid colon, or urinary bladder, forms a posterior component of the sac wall.

viva.q: What anatomical landmark confirms that a herniotomy dissection has reached the true high neck of the sac?
viva.a: Exposure of the extraperitoneal fat pad and visualization of the deep inferior epigastric vessels immediately medial to the neck of the sac.

image.brief: Formalin-fixed specimen jar containing an excised 7 cm pearly-white, glistening fibrous peritoneal hernial sac with a narrow neck, wider body, and rounded blind fundus.

items.summary: Excision specimen of stripped long saphenous vein showing an elongated, tortuous, thick-walled venous trunk with focal saccular dilatations.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Long, cord-like, cylindrical venous vessel measuring 30 to 45 cm in length representing the stripped great (long) saphenous vein.
Markedly tortuous and irregular course with alternating segments of thick-walled muscular hypertrophy and thin-walled saccular dilatations.
Luminal aspect reveals attenuated, stretched, or completely incompetent bicuspid venous valve leaflets.
Cut section demonstrates phlebosclerosis: eccentric fibrous thickening of the intima and medial muscular hypertrophy.
Small side branches corresponding to avulsed tributary veins along the length of the vein.

blocks.title: Pathophysiology and venous hypertension
bullets: Primary varicose veins result from inherent venous wall weakness and primary valve incompetence at the saphenofemoral junction (SFJ).
Incompetence allows retrograde gravitational reflux of blood from the high-pressure femoral vein into the superficial saphenous trunk.
Chronic ambulatory venous hypertension produces capillary leakage of fibrinogen and extravasation of red blood cells into dermis.
Breakdown of red blood cells releases haemosiderin, producing brown pigmentation, lipodermatosclerosis, and venous ulceration.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Brodie-Trendelenburg test and duplex venous ultrasonography evaluate saphenofemoral competence and deep venous patency.
Traditional surgery: Trendelenburg high flush ligation of the SFJ with stripping of the vein down to the knee (avoiding saphenous nerve).
Modern endovenous thermal ablation (EVLA) or radiofrequency ablation (RFA) has largely superseded open surgical stripping.

viva.q: Why is the great saphenous vein stripped only down to the knee level rather than the ankle?
viva.a: Below the knee, the saphenous nerve runs in intimate anatomical contact with the vein; stripping below the knee risks permanent saphenous neuropathy and numbness.

viva.q: What causes the brown cutaneous pigmentation in the gaiter area in chronic varicose veins?
viva.a: Venous hypertension forces erythrocytes through widened endothelial junctions into the dermis; macrophage degradation of haemoglobin produces haemosiderin deposition.

viva.q: What is the critical surgical prerequisite that must be confirmed before stripping or ablating superficial varicose veins?
viva.a: Confirmation of deep venous patency (using duplex ultrasound or Perthes test) to ensure the deep veins can handle venous return from the lower limb.

image.brief: Gross pathology jar showing a 35 cm stripped long saphenous vein specimen displaying marked tortuosity, thick-walled segments, and irregular bulbous dilatations.

title.en: Dry gangrene of the foot and toes

items.summary: Amputated foot or toe specimen displaying shrivelled, hard, mummified black necrotic tissue with a sharp inflammatory line of demarcation.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Distal extremity (toes, forefoot) is shrunken, shrivelled, hard, and desiccated, resembling the tissue of an Egyptian mummy.
Distinct jet-black colouration resulting from the action of hydrogen sulphide on iron liberated from decomposing haemoglobin (iron sulphide).
Sharp, distinct, hyperaemic red line of demarcation clearly separating the dead mummified tissue from viable proximal skin.
Dry, non-tender, cold, and entirely devoid of putrefactive foul odour, crepitus, or purulent exudation.

blocks.title: Etiology and pathophysiology
bullets: Caused by gradual, progressive arterial occlusion in an extremity with preserved or adequate venous drainage.
Commonest causes: atherosclerosis obliterans (senile gangrene), Buerger disease (thromboangiitis obliterans), and Raynaud disease.
Fluid from dead tissue evaporates into the atmosphere faster than it can be replaced by occluded arterial inflow, preventing bacterial growth.
Pathologically represents pure coagulative necrosis of tissues without significant secondary bacterial putrefaction.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Line of demarcation is formed by a zone of active granulation tissue with polymorphs and capillary proliferation.
Dry gangrene may convert into wet gangrene if secondary bacterial infection is introduced by soaking or unsterile trauma.
Autoamputation can occur spontaneously over time; surgical amputation is performed proximal to the line of demarcation.

viva.q: What gives dry gangrene its characteristic jet-black colour?
viva.a: Haemoglobin from decomposing red blood cells breaks down, releasing iron that reacts with hydrogen sulphide produced by tissue proteolysis to form black iron sulphide.

viva.q: What is the physiological line of demarcation in dry gangrene?
viva.a: A hyperaemic zone of acute inflammatory granulation tissue where active polymorphs and capillaries digest and separate living tissue from dead necrotic tissue.

viva.q: Why does dry gangrene not develop foul-smelling putrefaction like wet gangrene?
viva.a: Because slow arterial occlusion with intact venous drainage allows tissue fluids to evaporate, producing dry desiccated tissue that inhibits bacterial multiplication.

image.brief: Amputation specimen jar of distal forefoot and toes displaying black, shrivelled, mummified dry gangrene with a sharp, distinct hyperaemic line of demarcation.

title.en: Wet gangrene of the lower extremity

items.summary: Amputated lower extremity specimen exhibiting swollen, oedematous, foul-smelling, putrefied dark greenish-black tissue with blebs and ill-defined margins.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Tissues are markedly swollen, soft, edematous, boggy, and discoloured with mixed dark green, purple, and black hues.
Extensive cutaneous bullae and blister formation containing foul-smelling, turbid, blood-stained serosanguinous fluid.
Skin exhibits extensive sloughing, liquefactive breakdown, and ulceration exposing underlying necrotic tendons and bone.
Conspicuous absence of a sharp, clear line of demarcation; inflammatory erythema and oedema spread proximally without clear margin.

blocks.title: Pathophysiology and bacterial putrefaction
bullets: Occurs in tissues where arterial occlusion is combined with impaired venous drainage or in moisture-rich diabetic soft tissues.
Virulent polymicrobial bacterial infection (coliforms, Bacteroides, staphylococci, streptococci, and putrefactive clostridia).
Bacteria proliferate rapidly in warm, moist, nutrient-rich dead tissue, releasing putrefactive enzymes that cause liquefactive necrosis.
Classic surgical setting is the infected neuro-ischaemic diabetic foot, bedsores, strangulated hernia, and acute arterial embolism.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Systemic toxaemia and septic shock develop rapidly due to massive absorption of bacterial endotoxins and tissue breakdown products.
Requires emergency resuscitation, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, and urgent surgical debridement or guillotine amputation.
Never treat wet gangrene conservatively; failure to decompress and debride promptly leads to fatal systemic sepsis.

viva.q: Why is there no sharp line of demarcation in wet gangrene?
viva.a: Because virulent bacterial putrefaction and liquefactive necrosis outpace the host's inflammatory response, rapidly tracking along tissue and fascial planes.

viva.q: Why is wet gangrene a surgical emergency compared to dry gangrene?
viva.a: Because active polymicrobial bacterial proliferation in moist necrotic tissue leads to rapid absorption of toxins, severe systemic toxaemia, septic shock, and death.

viva.q: What are the common clinical predisposing conditions for wet gangrene?
viva.a: Poorly controlled diabetes mellitus with infected foot ulcers, acute complete arterial occlusion with venous blockage, bedsores, and strangulated bowel.

image.brief: Amputated lower limb specimen displaying swollen, boggy, dark green-black putrefied foot tissue with burst skin blebs, sloughing, and spreading proximal erythema without demarcation.
